# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

content.content:
1	# Task dispatch without slots — the work-item queue
2	
3	The mechanism lives in [`engine/scheduler/queue/`](../../engine/scheduler/queue/),
4	behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`. A continuation of the owner's sketch (2026-08-12, reproduced in Appendix A), played against twenty timed
5	scenarios ([SCENARIOS.md](SCENARIOS.md)) and the field's prior art
6	([RESEARCH.md](RESEARCH.md)), with the owner's eight decisions of 2026-08-13
7	recorded in §15 and folded into the sections they changed. The phase plan
8	belongs to a tracking issue, not here. It supersedes
9	the slot machinery of
10	[per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3–§5](../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md) and
11	amends several of its §12 decisions (each amendment is named where it happens).
12	What it does **not** touch: the task folder anatomy (§1), the precondition
13	contract, code-work and its secrets model
14	([task-code-work DESIGN](../task-code-work/DESIGN.md)), the outcome ceiling, the
15	security posture (the issue is data; behavior comes from tracked files), and the
16	usage-metrics records.
17	
18	The shape in one paragraph: **work items are issues, available for work; any
19	number of executors pull from them.** A thin generator tick gives every
20	recurring task a standing work item at its anchor and flips blocked items
21	ready — pure label mechanics, no preconditions, no signals. An executor — a
22	GitHub Action by default, but anything that can read issues — picks up the
23	next ready item, claims it by label, evaluates the precondition (the only
24	place it ever runs): on a go it runs the work step and hands off to agentic work (a
25	CCR session invoked by API); on a no-go the item **rolls** — stamped
26	not-before the task's next anchor, blocked, reason recorded — so the item
27	itself carries "asked, declined, wakes at T". Follow-ups, fan-outs, urgency,
28	and one-off forcing are all just *creating or waking work items*. There is no
29	slot id, no run-ledger watermark, no exclusive claim, and no label-event
30	re-arm.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 1. What the slot machinery costs today
35	
36	The current design is push-shaped: one hourly scheduler run decides, at a single
37	instant, everything that will happen — which tasks are due, whether they run,
38	what they may touch — and encodes the decision into dispatch issues that a
39	label-event-triggered session then executes. Every complication below is a
40	consequence of that shape.
41	
42	- **The slot id is state smuggled into a title token.** `d2026-08-12`,
43	  `h2026-08-12T14Z`, `m2026-08` exist so that a scheduled occurrence has an
44	  identity — which the exactly-once guard needs (title search per slot), the
45	  stale backstop needs (the *leading character* of the slot id is parsed back
46	  into a period, `SLOT_PERIOD_MS`), and forcing needs (the `~f<runId>` marker
47	  appended so an operator re-run of an already-run slot isn't silently
48	  swallowed). Three mechanisms each decode a fragment of scheduler state out of
49	  a string in an issue title.
50	
51	- **Due-ness lives in a platform side channel.** "Has this slot run?" is
52	  answered by the Actions run ledger of the scheduler workflow itself
53	  (`lastSuccessTime`) — a watermark that is not visible beside the work, must
54	  exclude forced runs to stay correct, and whose unreadability has to fail the
55	  whole run (an exit-0 abort would advance it past slots it never evaluated).
56	  The state the system actually cares about — *was this occurrence's work
57	  created?* — is derivable from the issues themselves, and nothing reads it
58	  from there. *(A first cut of the go/no-go ruling briefly reintroduced a
59	  ledger read; the standing-item model (§5) removed it again — the tick is
60	  now a pure function of the clock and the issue list.)*
61	
62	- **A decision made at one instant cannot express ordering, only simultaneity.**
63	  The nightly chain's ordering is faked by anchor-hour staggering, which
64	  collapses whenever GitHub fires the cron late — hence the `exclusive: true`
65	  claim, a task-level hack whose cost is real: **a deferred slot is spent, not
66	  queued**, so a claim on the wrong night silently halves throughput. The
67	  system has no way to say "run B after A"; it can only say "run A alone".
68	
69	- **Label-event invocation is lossy, and the loss shaped three mechanisms.**
70	  The executor routine fires only on a fresh `labeled` event; a lost delivery
71	  leaves an armed issue sitting forever. So: the janitor's re-arm
72	  (remove/re-add the label to emit a new event), the 20-minute grace window so
73	  a re-arm never hands a live session a rival, and the stale escalation that
74	  bounds the re-arm loop. The claim protocol then has to survive *duplicate*
75	  events (the read-swap-confirm lease). All of it is compensation for a trigger
76	  that neither confirms delivery nor can be polled.
77	
78	- **Capacity, urgency, and follow-ups have no home.** There is exactly one
79	  implicit executor per repo and no way to add another; nothing distinguishes
80	  urgent work from routine work; a task cannot schedule a successor ("validate
81	  in two days what tonight's run delivered") except by hoping a future
82	  precondition rediscovers the situation. Forcing (`FORCE_TASKS`) is a special
83	  engine path with its own exemptions (skips preconditions, exempt from
84	  deferral, excluded from the watermark, slot-id marker) — where "run this now"
85	  ought to be the system's most ordinary operation.
86	
87	- **Visibility is split three ways.** Whether something *will* run is ledger
88	  math nobody can see; whether it *is* running is labels on an issue; what it
89	  *did* is a record line in a captured transcript. There is no one place where
90	  the state of the repo's recurring work can be read.
91	
92	What is worth keeping — and this design keeps all of it — is everything the
93	incidents taught: one session executes exactly one item and never sweeps the
94	queue (the duplicate-execution bug, DESIGN §5), the claim is a verified lease,
95	the issue is data and never instructions, behavior-defining content comes only
96	from tracked files, every exit converges to one visible terminal state, and
97	recovery lives in one place, in code.
98	
99	## 2. The shape — a pull-based queue of work items
100	
101	Four roles, strictly separated (this refines, rather than replaces, the
102	2026-08-06 three-responsibility split — the scheduler's job splits in two and
103	shrinks):
104	
105	1. **The generator** — a thin scheduled tick (the repo's one cron, unchanged
106	   rule). Three jobs, all deterministic label mechanics over the issue list:
107	   *instantiate* each recurring task's standing item when its time comes,
108	   *ready* blocked items whose dependencies have resolved and whose not-before
109	   has passed, and *reclaim* dead executor claims. It evaluates no
110	   preconditions and collects no signals (§5); it executes nothing.
111	2. **Executors** — any number of pull workers. Each iteration: pick the next
112	   ready item (urgent first), claim it, evaluate the precondition — the only
113	   place it is ever evaluated — then on a go run the work step and either finish
114	   (agentless task) or invoke the agentic phase and hand the item to it; on a
115	   no-go, roll a scheduled item to its next anchor (§5). An executor is
116	   platform-agnostic by construction: its whole interface is issue read/write
117	   plus the repo at HEAD. More capacity = more executors.
118	3. **Agents** — CCR sessions, one per handed-off item, invoked by the executor.
119	   An agent executes its one item's task file, verifies its outcome ceiling,
120	   and converges the item to a terminal state.
121	4. **The janitor** — unchanged in role, smaller in scope: dead executor claims,
122	   dead agent claims, stale-item escalation, queue health review. The re-arm
123	   retires (§11).
124	
125	The queue itself is the repo's issues, and under the standing-item model that
126	sentence is complete: everything the system knows — including "this task was
127	asked, declined, and wakes again at T" — is on a work item. No plan file, no
128	watermark, no ledger read. The tick is a pure function of the clock and the
129	issue list; which is what the sketch means by *visibility into state*.
130	
131	## 3. The work item
132	
133	An issue, `[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>` (plus an optional free-form
134	qualifier after the task, for tasks that legitimately have several concurrent
135	items — a fan-out names its target: `[claudinite-work] sheepdog/fleet-baseline
136	member-repo-x`). **The issue number is the identity.** No slot id: an
137	occurrence needs no name beyond the item that embodies it, and everything the
138	slot id encoded is recovered elsewhere — dedup from the family's creation
139	timestamps (§5), staleness from the task's own declared frequency read at HEAD
140	(§11), forcing from the fact that creating an item *is* forcing (§8).
141	
142	Body, machine-first (same parsing discipline as today's dispatch body — the
143	first line is the task path, validated in code before anything trusts it):
144	
145	```
146	.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/task.md
147	
148	Not-before: 2026-08-14T04:00Z            # optional — see §9
149	Blocked-by: #812, #813                   # optional — see §9
150	
151	Execute the Claudinite task above.
152	The Context section below is binding scope — do not re-decide it.
153	
154	### Context
155	- <the creating precondition's binding lines, verbatim — unchanged>
156	
157	### Delivered by code-work
158	- <written by the executor at hand-off, unchanged shape>
159	```
160	
161	Everything behavior-defining — model, outcome ceiling, worker content, the
162	work step's command — is still read from the tracked task files at HEAD, never from the
163	issue. A work item whose task the repo no longer carries is closed as obsolete,
164	exactly like today's exit-14.
165	
166	**Origin marker.** Items the generator creates carry `origin:schedule`; items
167	created by hand, by a task, or by a fan-out do not, and an item adopted from a
168	marked issue carries `origin:request` (§16.3). The generator's dedup
169	guards (§5) count only `origin:schedule` items, so scheduled work and ad-hoc
170	work never suppress each other — a pending follow-up does not silence tomorrow's
171	occurrence, and an urgent hand-created item does not consume it either. A task
172	whose precondition should care about open follow-ups can see them through the
173	`issues` signal, as task-specific logic where it belongs.
174	
175	## 4. The state machine
176	
177	```
178	                     ┌────────────► closed  outcome:obsolete
179	                     │                    (precondition no longer holds; task gone)
180	 created ─► task:blocked ─► task:ready ─► task:executing ─► task:agent ─► closed  outcome:done
181	            (only when       (queue)       (claimed by an     (handed to        open    needs-human
182	             Blocked-by /                   executor)          a CCR session)           + one of the four
183	             Not-before                                                                   triage sub-labels
184	             present)
185	```
186	
187	Labels, the full vocabulary:
188	
189	| label | means | applied by |
190	|---|---|---|
191	| `task:blocked` | waiting on `Blocked-by` issues and/or `Not-before` | creator |
192	| `task:ready` | available for pickup | creator or the tick |
193	| `task:urgent` | modifier: pick before any non-urgent item | creator (write-gated, like every label) |
194	| `task:executing` | an executor holds the claim | executor, on claim |
195	| `task:agent` | an agent session owns it | executor, at hand-off |
196	| `outcome:done` | succeeded; nothing pending (closed) | executor or agent |
197	| `outcome:delivered` | **retired 2026-08-19, still read.** Meant "succeeded and left a live artifact the world still has to act on"; an unmerged PR now parks at `task:needs-human-approval` instead of closing, and nothing else ever wrote it. Closed issues carrying it are stored data, so every decoder still recognises it | — (historical) |
198	| `outcome:obsolete` | never ran: the pickup-time precondition said no, or the task is gone from the repo (closed as not planned) | executor |
199	| `needs-human` | parked for a human — the one triage *state*, and what every guard, sweep and dashboard turns on (open) | anyone, incl. janitor |
200	| `task:needs-human-action` | …and something outside the code must change first: a secret set, a scope granted, a routine rewired, an input supplied | anyone, incl. janitor |
201	| `task:needs-human-decision` | …and the run stopped mid-flight, so the next step is a choice: re-queue or abandon, does the half-done work stand, was the ceiling violation acceptable | anyone, incl. janitor |
202	| `task:needs-human-approval` | …and it **succeeded**, deliberately leaving an unmerged PR. The one park that is not a fault | executor or agent |
203	| `task:needs-human-failure` | …and the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or forged item. The default when nothing else fits | anyone, incl. janitor |
204	
205	**Every park wears two labels**: `needs-human` *and* exactly one sub-label. The
206	state and the routing are different questions — the machine reads the first, a
207	person reads the second — and collapsing them would have meant a migration to
208	land rather than an additive write (the collapse is #1050's, once the fleet has
209	converged past the split).
210	
211	**A park wearing no sub-label reads as `failure`.** That is the compatibility
212	direction chosen deliberately: every item an engine older than the split left
213	behind, and every kind word a newer engine invents that this one does not know,
214	holds the lane rather than silently letting a broken task keep filing work.
215	
216	**Only a `failure` park holds the task's lane** (§5). An open `origin:schedule`
217	item *is* the task's standing item, so while one exists no further occurrence is
218	filed — for a break that is the point, since a queue of items that will fail the
219	same way helps nobody and the silence is the signal. For the other three it is a
220	bug: a PR waiting on a reviewer, a decision waiting on its owner and a secret
221	waiting to be set are one person's inbox, not a fault in the task, and #1032
222	measured what conflating them costs — a permission gap parked `missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
223	`fleet-digest` for two days while its dashboard read healthy, because no item was
224	ever filed behind the parked one. So the generator drops non-blocking parks from
225	both the standing-item test and the duplicate sweep beside it.
226	
227	This is the sketch's lifecycle with two adjustments, both argued for rather
228	than assumed:
229	
230	- **Executor identity is a claim comment, not a label.** The sketch's
231	  `being-handled-by-executor-1` puts an unbounded set (executor identities) into
232	  a vocabulary that must stay small and queryable; every new executor would mint
233	  a label, and a query for "what is executing" would have to know every
234	  executor's name. One state label (`task:executing`) answers the query; the
235	  claim comment — which the lease protocol requires anyway — carries *who*
236	  (executor id, run URL) and *when*. Same for `task:agent`: the hand-off
237	  comment names the CCR session.
238	- **`succeeded-with-unexpected-result` became `outcome:delivered`, and then
239	  became a park.** "Unexpected" would blur two things that must not blur: a run
240	  that legitimately left a pending artifact within its ceiling (open-pr task →
241	  open PR: *expected*, but the world hasn't finished with it), and a run that
242	  violated its ceiling (a `none` task that opened a PR). The second is still a
243	  **failure**, now `task:needs-human-decision` — someone must say whether the
244	  overreach stands — exactly as `verify-outcome` enforces. The first turned out
245	  not to be a terminal state at all: a PR nobody has merged is waiting on a
246	  named person, and closing the item hid that from every surface that counts
247	  open work, so it parks at `task:needs-human-approval` and stays open. It does
248	  not hold the lane, so the reviewer's silence delays only the review.
249	
250	Terminal-state discipline is unchanged: every item converges exactly once to
251	exactly one end — one of the two closes, or a park under one of the four
252	sub-labels — with one comment saying what happened.
253	
254	**Label writes are granular, always** ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2): add and
255	remove named labels (REST POST/DELETE), never write the label *set* (PUT,
256	GraphQL `updateIssue`) — a set-write replaces from a stale snapshot and
257	clobbers concurrent transitions, a bug class GitHub's own CLI shipped
258	([cli/cli#4861](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/4861)). With multiple
259	executors and a tick all moving labels, this is a correctness rule, not a
260	style preference.
261	
262	**The road back from `needs-human`** (SCENARIOS S12/S19, F7): a human who has
263	resolved the cause re-queues the item by removing `needs-human` and its
264	sub-label and applying `task:ready` — the sanctioned retry lever, write-gated like every label
265	operation here. The next pickup re-runs the precondition (§6.4), which is what
266	makes the retry safe even when the failed run half-did its work. Alternatively
267	the human closes the item (optionally superseding it with a forced retry,
268	§8); nothing mechanical ever re-queues a `needs-human` item.
269	
270	## 5. The generator — the standing work item
271	
272	> Amended 2026-08-18 (§16.3): the tick has a **fourth** job, `adopt` — an ordinary
273	> issue marked `claude-task` becomes a work item, and the mark is consumed in the
274	> same pass. It is the same kind of job as the other three: label mechanics over
275	> the issue list, no precondition, no signal.
276	
277	**The tick never evaluates a precondition and never collects a signal**
278	(owner model, 2026-08-13). Creation is calendar-only: at a task's anchor, the
279	tick creates its work item *unconditionally* — the precondition speaks later,
280	at pickup, on the executor (§6.4), which is where the original sketch had it
281	all along. What happens on a no-go is the model's whole trick: the item is
282	**not closed** — the executor stamps it `Not-before: <the task's next anchor>`,
283	swaps it back to `task:blocked`, records the reason, and the item **rolls
284	forward**. The next anchor readies it again; the next pick re-asks. One ask
285	per period, exactly — go/no-go preserved — and the memory of "evaluated,
286	declined, ask again at T" is carried **on the item itself**, in the one place
287	this design keeps state.
288	
289	```text
290	tick(now):
291	  if dormant: return                            # before any read, as today
292	
293	  # ---- job 1: instantiate (calendar-only; no preconditions, no signals) ----
294	  for task in discoverTasks():                  # NO ordering requirement — the
295	    if task.frequency == 'manual': continue     # `after` yield is pick-time (§6.1)
296	    A = mostRecentAnchor(task.frequency, config.taskScheduler, now)
297	    family = issues(title == "[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>",
298	                    label "origin:schedule", state ALL)
299	                    # REST issue list, never the search index (S6/F11)
300	    # A park that is somebody's INBOX rather than a fault does not hold the
301	    # lane: it is neither the standing item nor a duplicate of one, so it drops
302	    # out of the two OPEN tests below and the schedule goes on around it. A
303	    # `failure` park, and any park an older engine left unclassified, stays in
304	    # (§4). It stays in `family` for the occurrence guard further down, which is
305	    # the point: the parked item DID consume its own occurrence, so the next
306	    # item is filed at the next anchor and not immediately.
307	    live = [i for i in family if not (i has "needs-human" and not blockingPark(i))]
308	    # F16 self-heal first: nothing documents that a REST list from another
309	    # node sees a creation seconds old, so a stale list can let a duplicate
310	    # standing item through. Assume it will happen rather than that it won't:
311	    # close every open family item but the OLDEST, outcome:obsolete, with a
312	    # dedupe comment. Serialized by the tick's concurrency group.
313	    if count(i.state == OPEN for i in live) > 1: closeAllButOldest(live)
314	    if any(i.state == OPEN for i in live):      continue  # the standing item
315	                                                          # already exists
316	    # the occurrence guard has TWO halves (F13, caught by the simulator): an
317	    # item CREATED at-or-after A covers this occurrence — and so does an item
318	    # CLOSED at-or-after A, because a rolled item created in an earlier
319	    # period that ran and closed today consumed today's occurrence. With the
320	    # created_at half alone, the very next tick after such a close creates a
321	    # second item for the same occurrence: a double execution.
322	    if any(i.created_at >= A or i.closed_at >= A for i in family): continue
323	    createIssue(title:  "[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>",
324	                body:   taskPath,
325	                labels: ["origin:schedule",
326	                         family.isEmpty ? "task:blocked" : "task:ready"])
327	                # a brand-new task's FIRST item is born blocked with
328	                # Not-before = its next anchor — adoption must not fire
329	                # weekly/monthly tasks off-anchor (the old first-run concern)
330	
331	  # ---- job 2: ready whatever is due --------------------------------------
332	  for item in issues(label "task:blocked", state OPEN):   # any origin
333	    {blockedBy, notBefore} = parseBody(item)
334	    if all(issues(blockedBy).state == CLOSED) and now >= notBefore:
335	      swapLabel(item, "task:blocked" -> "task:ready")
336	
337	  # ---- job 3: reclaim dead executor claims (§11) --------------------------
338	  for item in issues(label "task:executing", state OPEN):
339	    if noActivitySince(item, EXECUTING_LEASH): stripToReady(item, comment)
340	```
341	
342	And the roll, executor-side (the full pick flow is §6):
343	
344	```text
345	on pick, verdict = precondition(signals, config):
346	  go     -> proceed (work step, hand-off, converge, CLOSE with an outcome)
347	  no-go  -> item carries origin:schedule?
348	              yes: Not-before = nextAnchor(task.frequency); ready -> blocked;
349	                   record the reason            # the item ROLLS — not an exit
350	              no:  close outcome:obsolete       # an ad-hoc item has no next
351	                                                # anchor to roll to (S17)
352	```
353	
354	**What this dissolves, all at once:**
355	
356	- **The evaluate-once ledger.** No `lastTick`, no Actions-ledger read, no
357	  grace fallback: "was this occurrence evaluated" is answered by the standing
358	  item's own `Not-before`. §1's side-channel complaint is fully satisfied
359	  again — the tick is a pure function of the clock and the issue list.
360	- **The 24-attempts cost (F10).** The tick evaluates nothing; the precondition
361	  runs once per wake, i.e. once per period per task. Signals are collected by
362	  the executor for the one picked task — the tick performs no GitHub reads
363	  beyond the issue list.
364	- **Declined occurrences were invisible in every earlier model** — no-go
365	  meant no item (or a ledger entry nobody sees). Now a quiet task's item shows
366	  its last ask, its reason, and its next wake, on its timeline. This closes
367	  the last gap in the sketch's *visibility into state*.
368	- **Forcing needs no item creation in the common case** (§8): the standing
369	  item exists, so force = wake it — strip `task:blocked`, clear `Not-before`,
370	  optionally add `task:urgent`. The same lever as the human re-queue (§4),
371	  which is no accident.
372	- **F9 (topological creation order) retires unbuilt**: `after` no longer
373	  wires `Blocked-by` at creation — see §6.1/§9 — so the tick's iteration
374	  order stops mattering.
375	
376	**Titles carry no timestamp, and never will** (owner question, answered
377	plainly): every item of a task shares the bare title `[claudinite-work]
378	<pack>/<task>`; successive items are told apart by issue number, which is the
379	identity (§3). The optional qualifier exists only for deliberately concurrent
380	items (fan-out targets). Nothing ever parses a date out of a title — that was
381	the slot grammar, and it stays dead.
382	
383	**The costs, named:**
384	
385	- **The issue list's baseline changes meaning.** A quiet repo used to show
386	  zero open scheduler issues; now it shows one open (blocked) item per
387	  scheduled task, each stating its next wake. That is ~a dozen standing open
388	  issues here — read it as the dashboard it is: the issue list *is* the
389	  scheduler's state, which is what the sketch asked for. Filtering them out
390	  of "real issues" views is one label query (`-label:origin:schedule`).
391	- **Hourly tasks churn their item.** An hourly task that stays no-go rolls
392	  ~24 times a day: two label flips and a body edit per roll, on one issue.
393	  Cheap against API quotas, noisy on that item's timeline; the roll writes no
394	  comment (the `Not-before` bump is the record) so the noise is timeline
395	  events, not comment spam. Named and accepted — one issue absorbs it.
396	- **A long-quiet task's item lives for months.** That is the feature wearing
397	  its cost: the item is the task's standing status line, and its age is
398	  information ("quiet since June"), not staleness — the janitor's stale rule
399	  keys on `task:ready` age, which a properly rolling item never accumulates.
400	
401	**Errored and forced items against the guards** (unchanged in substance from
402	the earlier draft, restated for the new shape):
403	
404	- A **failed run** parks its item open + `needs-human` (a real exit — the
405	  roll is only for no-go verdicts, never for failures). A `failure` park *is*
406	  the backlog guard: no new item until a human closes or re-queues it — one
407	  broken task, one triage item, however long it takes. The other three
408	  sub-labels are **not** guards (§4): a park that only wants a reviewer, a
409	  decision or a secret leaves the lane open, so the next occurrence is filed
410	  beside it on schedule. It still consumes its own occurrence, so nothing is
411	  filed until that next anchor.
412	- A **forced ad-hoc item** (no `origin:schedule`) is invisible to both
413	  guards in both directions, whatever state it ends in — it neither
414	  suppresses nor consumes an occurrence (#749's property, kept).
415	- **Force-of-a-scheduled-task** is now the wake lever, not an item (§8), so
416	  the S15 same-title collision cannot arise from the common force at all; the
417	  pick mutex (§6.1) still covers a deliberately created concurrent item.
418	
419	## 6. The executor — pick up, claim, prepare, hand off
420	
421	An executor iteration, in code end to end (the reference implementation is a
422	job in the vendored workflow, triggered by `issues: labeled [task:ready]`
423	events for latency **and** by the tick's cron as the poll that makes lost
424	events irrelevant; `workflow_dispatch` for a hand-started drain):
425	
426	1. **Pick**: list open `task:ready` items; `task:urgent` first, then
427	   **random order among the ready** (owner decision, 2026-08-15). Two
428	   executors listing the same queue then contend on *different* heads
429	   instead of cascading down one — and nothing leans on oldest-first: the
430	   stale-ready escalation is period-scale (~2 periods), indifferent to the
431	   minute-scale reordering a shuffle introduces. Two skip rules, both live
432	   reads at pick time:
433	   - **Same-title mutex** (SCENARIOS S15/F6): skip an item whose exact title
434	     (task + qualifier) has another open item in `task:executing` or
435	     `task:agent` — one task, one execution at a time; a fan-out's distinct
436	     qualifiers still parallelize. The skipped item is picked once its twin
437	     converges.
438	   - **The `after` yield** (SCENARIOS S24): skip a scheduled item whose task
439	     declares `after: [T]` while T's standing item is `task:ready`,
440	     `task:executing`, or `task:agent` — yield *while the upstream is live
441	     this cycle*, nothing more. A rolled upstream (blocked until its next
442	     anchor: it declined this cycle) does not block, and neither does one
443	     sitting `needs-human` — a broken upstream must not halt its dependents
444	     indefinitely, the same bound the old exclusive claim drew at three days.
445	     This is deliberately **not** a `Blocked-by` edge: a standing item that
446	     rolls never closes, so wiring `after` as blocked-by-the-item would
447	     starve every dependent of a quiet upstream forever — the one real trap
448	     in the standing-item model, caught in replay (S24).
449	
450	   **The filters are advisory at pick time (F15)**: they read possibly-stale
451	   state, so two executors can pass them simultaneously and claim
452	   *different* items the filters should have serialized — a twin pair, or an
453	   upstream and its dependent. The per-item lease cannot see this (it
454	   protects one item, not one title). So after **winning** a claim, the
455	   executor re-verifies the filters against live state; if a conflicting
456	   item now holds an **earlier** claim (comment order — the same arbiter the
457	   lease trusts), it reverts its own claim to `task:ready` and moves on.
458	   Bounded (one revert per conflict), deterministic (comment order), and
459	   the earlier claim never notices (S32).
460	
461	   Take the first survivor. None → exit quietly.
462	2. **Claim — the verified lease, unchanged in shape** (it earned its keep):
463	   read labels, abandon if `task:ready` is gone or `task:executing` /
464	   `task:agent` / `needs-human` present; swap `task:ready → task:executing` and
465	   post the claim comment (executor id, run URL, UTC time); re-read, earliest
466	   claim comment wins, loser reverts nothing and moves on — it may pick a
467	   *different* item and try again (an executor is code iterating a queue, not a
468	   session sweeping one; the one-session-one-issue rule binds agents, and each
469	   claimed item still gets exactly one agent). Three precisions the
470	   simulator's validation review forced (2026-08-13), each an implicit
471	   assumption made explicit:
472	   - **"Earliest" means lowest comment *id*, never timestamp** — GitHub
473	     comment `created_at` has one-second granularity, so simultaneous claims
474	     tie on time; comment ids are server-assigned and strictly increasing,
475	     a total order the protocol gets for free. Nothing in the lease may
476	     compare runner clocks.
477	   - **The arbiter is episode-scoped (F18)**: earliest claim comment **since
478	     the item last became ready** — the revert/reclaim/re-queue comment is
479	     the episode boundary. Over the item's lifetime, dead claims accumulate
480	     (every reclaim and revert leaves one behind); arbitrating over all of
481	     them makes a *dead* claim outrank every future live claimant, and the
482	     item livelocks through reclaim cycles forever. Caught by the simulator
483	     racing two executors onto a reverted item (S32) — and masked until
484	     then because a single executor beats its own stale claim by id
485	     equality.
486	   - **Letting go of an open item kills your claim (F24)**: the boundary is
487	     a *rule about every path that ends an episode*, not a property of the
488	     three that happened to write a comment. An executor that stops owning
489	     an item without closing it — the roll, every `needs-human` park, and a
490	     claimant that *lost* the arbitration — **strikes its own claim**,
491	     appending the episode marker to the claim comment it already wrote. The
492	     loser matters as much as the winner: its claim is younger than the
493	     winner's, so it survives the winner's own strike and becomes the
494	     earliest claim of the *next* episode, moving the livelock one episode
495	     along rather than removing it. That satisfies the boundary with no new
496	     timeline entry, which is what lets the roll keep its silence (§5); a
497	     marker *comment* there would put one on every declining hourly task,
498	     every hour. Only a claim's author strikes it, so a claim can be
499	     withdrawn but never forged earlier, and comment ids still give the
500	     total order. A successful hand-off does **not** strike — that episode
501	     is live, owned by the session — and a *dead* executor strikes nothing,
502	     which is the case the leash reclaim already covers.
503	   - **The label swap is two API calls, not a CAS** — GitHub has no atomic
504	     label swap. That is fine *because* labels are not the arbiter: they are
505	     visibility and the pick filter; the claim comments arbitrate, so a torn
506	     swap can never mint a second owner. What it *can* do — executor dies
507	     between the remove and the add — is leave an open item with **no state
508	     label at all**, invisible to every rule that filters by state. The
509	     janitor gains the repair (§11): an open work item wearing neither a
510	     `task:*` state nor `needs-human` is off the state machine entirely →
511	     `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-decision`, a human's to look at — which
512	     state it should have had is a judgement about what actually ran.
513	3. **Validate in code**: the body's first line is a legal task path, the file
514	   exists at HEAD, the pack is declared, `task.mjs` parses. Task gone → close,
515	   `outcome:obsolete`, comment. Malformed → `needs-human` +
516	   `task:needs-human-failure` (possible forgery, a human must see it),
517	   unchanged from today.
518	4. **Evaluate the precondition — the only place it ever runs** (the sketch's
519	   "evaluates preconditions", now literally once). Creation was calendar-only
520	   (§5), so this is not a re-check of anything — it is *the* verdict, over
521	   signals the executor collects for this one task. On **go**: proceed, with
522	   the verdict's Context written into the body as the agent's binding scope.
523	   On **no-go**: a scheduled item **rolls** — `Not-before` stamped with the
524	   task's next anchor, `task:ready → task:blocked`, the reason recorded — and
525	   an ad-hoc item (no `origin:schedule`, so no anchor to roll to) closes
526	   `outcome:obsolete` with the reason commented (a follow-up whose world
527	   settled on its own, S17). **This amends §12.3's "the precondition is the
528	   only decision point" by re-siting, not weakening it**: still exactly the
529	   precondition deciding, still one decision point — moved from the scheduler
530	   run to the pick — and the work step and the agent still may not skip; the
531	   doctrine's target (later phases inventing "new reasons to skip") is
532	   untouched.
533	
534	   **This stays clean only while preconditions ask task questions, not
535	   calendar ones** (owner's condition, 2026-08-13). "Is there work?" is a
536	   question about the world; "has it been more than a day?" is the scheduler's
537	   own question leaking into a task, and under this model it is doubly wrong —
538	   the item already *carries* its schedule in `Not-before`, so a calendar
539	   precondition would be a second clock disagreeing with the first. Timing
540	   belongs to `frequency`, the anchors, and `Not-before`. The rule is
541	   **advisory** by owner ruling: no mechanical check (the property is not
542	   checkable), and the residual exposure is an item rolled with a calendar
543	   reason in its record — visible, and it costs a cycle, not correctness. The one live offender is resolved by
544	   ruling rather than grandfathered: **baselining's `ageDays > 1` gate is
545	   dropped outright** (owner, 2026-08-13: "the wrong precondition"). Its
546	   precondition becomes the work question alone — is the mount behind canon
547	   head, are migration notes unapplied — with cadence carried by
548	   `frequency: daily-2h` and nothing else. The corpus enters the new mechanism
549	   with zero calendar preconditions.
550	5. **The work step**, Action-side, unchanged contract: subprocess, task dir
551	   cwd, `required_secrets` as env, timeout, `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`
552	   conditional hand-off. **This step is the work, not preparation for it**
553	   (owner correction, 2026-08-15): for most of the fleet it is the whole task —
554	   long-running, crash-prone, PR-creating — and the agent phase is the
555	   sometimes-important judgment minority. The contract key is still spelled
556	   `code_work` (renaming a vendored key is a migration, tracked separately);
557	   the design calls the phase what it is. Three requirements, the first
558	   stated explicitly since SCENARIOS S8/F12:
559	   - **Re-entrant** — a dead executor's claim is reclaimed and the item
560	     re-picked, so the work can run again over its own half-done output (it
561	     already must survive this today, where a scheduler run dying mid-work
562	     leaves the slot due; the contract just never said so).
563	   - **Heartbeat while it runs** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the
564	     executor comments on the item every ~15 minutes during the work step.
565	     The heartbeat is what lets one short global executing leash survive
566	     arbitrarily long work — the leash measures executor *death* (heartbeats
567	     stopped), never work *duration* — and it is the item's visibility during
568	     the hours its timeline would otherwise go dark (§11 has the leash
569	     arithmetic this replaces).
570	   - **The terminal comment is the durable record.** Actions logs expire; the
571	     item is what remains. Whatever ends the item — converge here, or the
572	     agent later — the closing comment carries the `claudinite-task-exec`
573	     record and every artifact the work created (PR links above all). For an
574	     agentless task this comment is the *only* durable trace of the run, which
575	     is what makes it non-optional.
576	
577	   Failure → comment + `needs-human` + a sub-label, `task:executing` removed —
578	   and **the worker chooses which sub-label**. The executor sees an exit code
579	   and nothing else, so it cannot tell a token missing a scope (a person's
580	   five-second fix) from an exception in the worker's own code (an afternoon);
581	   a worker that knows prints `claudinite-needs-human: <kind> — <detail>` on
582	   either stream before exiting non-zero and the park routes on it. Read from
583	   the output rather than a file, because it must survive the SIGKILL at
584	   `code_work_timeout` — output is echoed live, a file written at exit is never
585	   written at all. The last marker wins, so a sweep may revise its verdict as
586	   it works through its targets; no marker parks at `failure`, which is what
587	   every worker written before the marker existed does in every run.
588	
589	   Success, agentless task or no agent requested → converge now: `outcome:done`,
590	   close, done — the quiet-on-success property survives as a *closed* item
591	   rather than no item, which is the better trade: the run is now visible.
592	   **Unless the payload names an unmerged PR**, which is not a finished run but
593	   a waiting reviewer: that parks at `task:needs-human-approval`, open, and does
594	   not hold the lane.
595	6. **Hand off**: write `### Delivered by code-work` / `### Why the agent is
596	   here` into the body (unchanged shapes), swap `task:executing → task:agent`,
597	   post the hand-off comment carrying a fresh **invocation nonce**, then
598	   **fire the invocation endpoint exactly once** with a payload naming this
599	   issue and that nonce.
600	
601	   **Once per item, ever — and that one decision removes a whole protocol**
602	   (owner, 2026-08-15). An earlier draft retried a timed-out call and, because
603	   a client-side timeout may still have started a session, accepted
604	   at-least-once invocation and paid for it with an agent-side claim lease
605	   (§7) to collapse the duplicates. But a retry is only safe when you know the
606	   first call did nothing, and the timeout is exactly the case where you
607	   cannot know. Declining to retry keeps invocation **at-most-once**, so two
608	   sessions can never arrive at one item and the lease has nothing to collapse.
609	   The nonce survives, earning its keep differently: it proves a fire names
610	   *this* hand-off rather than a stale or replayed one.
611	
612	   Three outcomes, and the third is the whole point:
613	   - **fired** — a session exists; the item is the agent's.
614	   - **refused** (a status came back) — no session, and the cause is a token,
615	     a URL or a routine, which no retry fixes: converge `needs-human` +
616	     `task:needs-human-action` naming it.
617	   - **unanswered** (a timeout, a dropped connection) — the session may or may
618	     not exist, and nothing may guess. The item **stays** `task:agent` with a
619	     comment saying the outcome is unknown; whichever way it went is settled by
620	     a rule that already exists — a session that started converges the item, and
621	     one that never did leaves it silent until the janitor's agent leash (§11)
622	     brings it to triage. No new mechanism, no re-queue that could duplicate.
623	
624	   Either way a lost hand-off is a *synchronous, visible* event at the
625	   executor, not a silently missing label event (this is what retires the
626	   re-arm — §11, and the credential it costs is §12).
627	
628	**An executor run performs one item** — not a configured maximum but the
629	executor's essence (owner, 2026-08-15): claim it, see it through to its
630	settle (roll, close, hand-off, or failure), end. The run's `timeout-minutes`
631	sizes to a single work bound, a platform kill loses at most one item's
632	progress, and self-re-dispatch (§10) chains the rest at ~a minute of spin-up
633	per item. Each item's claim is independently leased, so executor concurrency
634	is safe at any width. The old
635	bound tying the run to its leash — `timeout-minutes` ≤ the executing leash, so
636	the platform killed a hung runner before its claim was reaped — **retires with
637	the heartbeat** (2026-08-15): it capped every run at under an hour, which the
638	work-as-work model cannot accept. The stalled-worker lesson
639	([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2) is now held by three smaller pieces instead: a
640	*dead* runner stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within ~the leash; a *wedged
641	work subprocess* is killed by the work's own declared timeout (the contract's
642	existing bound), after which the executor converges the failure; and a
643	*reclaimed-but-alive* runner abandons at its next transition, because the
644	executor re-verifies its own lease at every state change (§11). The run's
645	`timeout-minutes` is then sized to the work it may legally do — the largest
646	single work bound it can pick — not to the leash.
647	
648	**Idempotency, honestly (owner concern, 2026-08-13: "I'm not sure we can
649	guarantee all tasks to be idempotent").** Agreed — and the design does not
650	require it. The queue literature's blanket "make handlers idempotent" applies
651	to systems where duplicate *invocations* reach the handler; here the executor
652	claim collapses duplicate pickups **before work starts** (§6.2) and at-most-once
653	invocation means no duplicate ever reaches the agent hop (§6.6), so what tasks
654	must actually tolerate is much narrower:
655	
656	- **The work step must be re-entrant** — a *sequential* re-run after a
657	  crash-and-reclaim (§6.5). That is convergence ("check what exists, continue
658	  from there"), not idempotency, and it is already required of the work today.
659	  Concurrent overlap with a zombie run is excluded by the lease re-verify and
660	  the work's own timeout (above), not asked of the task.
661	- **Re-executed agent work passes through the precondition again** (§6.4),
662	  and the half-run's artifacts are on the item (Delivered section, the
663	  PR-number comments the agent posts as it works — the item is the run's own
664	  inbox/outbox). A re-pick therefore *sees* what already happened and
665	  converges `outcome:obsolete` instead of redoing it — check-before-act,
666	  carried by the mechanism, not by task-author discipline.
667	- The residual overlap cases are bounded by the **write ceiling**: the worst
668	  historical duplicate produced twin PRs — visible, closeable, never
669	  destructive.
670	
671	And for a task that can promise none of this — a genuinely one-shot side
672	effect (a store submission, an external notification, a payment-shaped
673	action): the contract gains **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`**
674	(default `'requeue'`). Declaring `'needs-human'` makes every recovery path
675	that would re-execute — leash reclaim (§11), the human re-queue lever (§4) —
676	converge to triage instead (`task:needs-human-decision`: whether the
677	interrupted run left anything behind is exactly the choice being handed over):
678	**at-most-once plus a human**. This is the ack-early/ack-late dial every queue exposes, and
679	Celery ships ack-early as its *default* precisely so non-idempotent tasks
680	are never silently re-run ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §1); here the safe-side
681	default stays `'requeue'` because most of this fleet's tasks are
682	sweep-shaped, and the one-shot minority declares itself. Running
683	more executors — a second workflow instance, a laptop, a k8s job — requires
684	only an issues-scope token; nothing about the queue knows how many exist.

686	## 7. The agent
687	
688	> Amended 2026-08-18 (§16.6): a session that picks up a request item validates the
689	> issue it names as well as the item, runs at the item's `Model:`, and writes the
690	> result back onto that issue when it parks for approval.
691	
692	Today's `executor.md` collapses: the trigger-identification dance
693	(`resolve-dispatch`'s not-mine / scope-mismatch / no-trigger / needs-issue
694	verdicts, the two transports, the no-fallback rule)
695	existed because the session had to *discover* which label event started it. An
696	invoked session is told its item in its prompt — one issue number — and the
697	prompt is written by executor code, not by a human. What survives, verbatim in
698	role: validate the item in code before acting (never trust the prompt more
699	than a label event — re-resolve the task path at HEAD), honor the Context as
700	binding scope, run `task.md` at the declared model with the declared timeout
701	stated plainly, verify the outcome ceiling in code (`verify-outcome`), converge
702	the item (`outcome:done`, or a park under one of the four sub-labels + comment),
703	print the `claudinite-task-exec` record, capture the session. One session, one
704	item, no queue awareness — unchanged, and now structural: the session never
705	receives a queue, only an item.
706	
707	**The agent does NOT claim** (owner, 2026-08-15 — reversing an earlier draft of
708	this section). A claim lease here would answer "two sessions arrived at one
709	item", and under at-most-once invocation (§6.6) that cannot happen: the endpoint
710	is called once per item and never retried, so there is no second session to
711	arbitrate against. Adding the lease anyway would be machinery maintaining a
712	property the caller already guarantees — and machinery that reads as a licence to
713	retry, which is what would break the guarantee.
714	
715	What the session does instead is **check, not claim**: before touching anything,
716	confirm in code that the item carries `task:agent` and that its newest hand-off
717	comment carries the nonce this fire was given. A mismatch means the fire names a
718	hand-off that is not the current one — a replay, or an episode that has since been
719	reclaimed — and the session stops without touching the item. One comparison, no
720	protocol, and it costs nothing when it passes.
721	
722	The session's instructions are themselves a tracked file
723	([`engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md`](../../engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md))
724	that the routine's stored prompt does nothing but point at, so the issue-is-data
725	posture holds at this hop too: the payload names an item, and every instruction
726	comes from a file under review.

728	## 8. Urgency and forcing — creating or waking an item is the whole mechanism
729	
730	- **Urgent** work is an item with `task:urgent`: picked first, and the
731	  `labeled` event gives it executor latency of one spin-up. Nothing else is
732	  special about it.
733	- **Forcing a scheduled task is waking its standing item** (owner model,
734	  2026-08-13). The item exists (§5), so force = strip `task:blocked` **and
735	  add `task:ready`**, clear `Not-before`, optionally add `task:urgent` — the
736	  same lever as the human re-queue (§4), which is no accident: "run this
737	  now" and "retry this now" are the same operation on the same object.
738	  `task:ready` is not bookkeeping: `pickOrder` (§6.1) admits on that label
739	  alone, so an item merely stripped of `task:blocked` wears no state any
740	  executor selects on, and the run reports `nothing ready to pick up` —
741	  indistinguishable from a healthy idle run. **When the standing item does
742	  not exist, forcing MINTS it** — a completed task closes its item and the
743	  next appears only at its anchor, so for most of a daily task's day there
744	  is nothing to wake, and refusing there would make a fleet-wide converge
745	  lever fail on most members most of the time. The minted item is an
746	  ordinary `origin:schedule` standing item: it consumes the current
747	  occurrence (so the tick does not create a second one beside it) and leaves
748	  the next anchor's alone. Cross-repo, the enforcer does not perform any of
749	  this itself; it dispatches the member's scheduler with a `wake` input and
750	  the member's own tick applies the recipe (§14). The executor evaluates the
751	  precondition at pick like always; a no-go rolls the item again with the
752	  reason on record, so a force that finds no work *says so* where the
753	  operator will read it. Truly unconditional force: say so in a Context line
754	  the task's precondition honors — but the default stands that even forced
755	  work is admitted by code. *(Deliberate divergence from #515's "forcing
756	  never consults the task"; its motivating case — the slot gate running
757	  before preconditions made mid-day forcing unreachable — does not exist
758	  here: nothing runs before the pick.)*
759	- **Forcing ad-hoc work is creating an item**: parameterized runs, `manual`
760	  tasks, fan-out targets. The CLI/composite (`create-work-item <pack>/<task>
761	  [--urgent] [--context …] [--supersedes #N]`) writes the generic "forced by
762	  hand — no precondition asserts there is work" Context; `--supersedes`
763	  additionally closes a named errored item as superseded by this retry. The
764	  CLI warns when an open same-title item exists — the pick-time mutex (§6.1)
765	  means the new item queues behind it, and the operator should know they are
766	  queueing, not jumping (SCENARIOS S15/F6). `FORCE_TASKS`, the
767	  forced-verdict path, the `~f` marker and the watermark exclusion all
768	  reduce to these two levers.
769	- **Cancelling one executor run means "move on", and the mechanism already
770	  reads it that way** (owner, 2026-08-16). A single cancellation is
771	  indistinguishable from a crash: the failure continuation (§10) keeps the
772	  train moving, and the cancelled run's item is freed by the leash. What a
773	  single cancellation can *never* mean is "stop the system" — the tick and
774	  events keep spawning runs — so that intent gets its own lever:
775	- **Suspending the whole queue is `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`** (owner,
776	  2026-08-16): a repo Actions **variable** (`vars.*`, stamped into each
777	  workflow's env by the wiring — settable in the UI or over the API, **no
778	  commit**), which every Claudinite workflow — tick and executor alike —
779	  checks as its *first act* and, when true, exits cleanly having fired
780	  nothing. The train parks at most one hop after suspension (an already
781	  in-flight continuation may fire one re-dispatch; that fresh run sees the
782	  variable and parks). Suspension gates workflow *starts* only: in-flight
783	  runs and agent sessions finish on their own — cancel those by hand if the
784	  hold is urgent — and items freeze exactly where they are, no labels
785	  touched, which is what makes the hold stateless. This is not dormancy:
786	  `dormant` is a *declared standing state* in tracked config, a commit,
787	  read by the same gates; the suspend variable is the instant, out-of-band
788	  operational hold. (S37.)
789	- **Resuming is clearing the variable — recovery needs no lever of its own.**
790	  The next cron tick performs the entire self-heal unaided: its reclaim job
791	  frees the claims of runs killed during the hold (their heartbeats long
792	  silent), its readiness job wakes whatever came due, and its drain picks the
793	  queue back up. An operator who won't wait the ≤1h dispatches the
794	  **scheduler** workflow by hand — the tick-plus-drain pair, *not* the bare
795	  executor, whose run would drain ready items but skip the reclaim/ready
796	  half that makes resume complete. (S38.)
797	- **`manual` tasks** are simply tasks the tick never instantiates: their items
798	  are only ever created by hand or by other tasks. The frequency token
799	  survives; the special-case slot resolution for it dies.
800	- **Fan-out across repos** is the enforcer creating one item per member repo
801	  (urgent when the pass is urgent) instead of firing member schedulers with
802	  `FORCE_TASKS` — same write-gated surface, and the fan-in below gives the
803	  enforcer something it never had: a status. Nothing about it is a "fleet
804	  mechanism": it is a task creating items, and if its work needs wider reach
805	  than the repo's ordinary sessions have, it names a wider invocation endpoint
806	  (§12).

808	## 9. Follow-ups, ordering, fan-in — the dependency fields
809	
810	`Blocked-by: #N[, #M…]` and `Not-before: <ISO instant>` on an item, evaluated
811	by the tick (§5). Three patterns fall out, all from the sketch:
812	
813	- **Follow-up validation.** A task whose run delivered something long-running
814	  (a store submission, an armed auto-merge, a real-world change that settles
815	  over days) ends `outcome:delivered` and creates its own follow-up item:
816	  `Blocked-by: #<this item>` (satisfied the moment this item closes) +
817	  `Not-before: <now + settle time>`. The tick readies it when the time passes;
818	  an executor then re-runs its precondition — which checks whether the world
819	  actually settled — and the item either runs, or closes obsolete because
820	  everything landed on its own. The "will anyone check tomorrow?" gap closes
821	  with machinery that is just two body fields.
822	- **Ordering, declared — the exclusive claim retires.** A task may declare
823	  `after: ['basics/baselining']` in `task.mjs`, and it compiles to the
824	  **pick-time yield** (§6.1), *not* to a `Blocked-by` edge: the executor
825	  skips the dependent while the upstream's standing item is live
826	  (ready/executing/agent) this cycle, and picks it the moment the upstream
827	  converges — or rolls. The distinction is load-bearing under the
828	  standing-item model: `Blocked-by` requires the blocker *closed*, and a
829	  standing item that rolls never closes, so wiring `after` as blocked-by
830	  would starve every dependent of a quiet upstream forever (S24 — the one
831	  trap found replaying the model). As a yield: on the late-fire night all
832	  chain items are created together, baselining runs first, extract and
833	  promote follow *the same night* in order; on the routine night where
834	  baselining's precondition declines and its item rolls, extract is pickable
835	  a minute later. Nothing is spent, no task claims a run, and the engine
836	  still never knows what baselining is — `after` names a task id, and the
837	  pick filter reads item states, generically. §12's exclusive-claim
838	  machinery (and its stated throughput cost) deletes. `Blocked-by` remains
839	  the right edge for what it is: dependencies on items that *terminate*
840	  (follow-ups, fan-ins).
841	- **Fan-out with a fan-in.** Fanning out is creating N items (§8). The fan-in
842	  is one more item — the status/aggregation task — created `Blocked-by` all N.
843	  It readies only when every child converged, and its precondition/work step read
844	  the children's outcome labels to report or escalate. "Getting the status of
845	  a fan-out" stops being a bespoke sweep and becomes an ordinary task whose
846	  edges the tick already evaluates.
847	
848	**Readiness has a second site: whoever closes an item re-checks its dependents
849	in code** (F1, reopened by the owner 2026-08-15 — reversing the 2026-08-13
850	decline, and amending §15.8's "dependency readiness is the tick's alone" in
851	siting, not in principle). On closing an item, the executor or agent doing the
852	closing evaluates every open `task:blocked` item naming it: `Blocked-by` all
853	closed and `Not-before` passed flips the dependent to `task:ready`, and a
854	drain follows — so a chain link or a fan-in proceeds within minutes of its
855	upstream converging instead of waiting out the tick. What changed since the
856	decline: under the work-as-work model the ~1h/link quantization stacks on
857	drain occupancy, so a three-link chain on a busy morning trailed into the
858	afternoon. The tick's readiness job stays exactly as it was, as the backstop —
859	a close by hand runs no engine code, and a missed re-check costs a tick of
860	latency, never correctness (SCENARIOS S33, and S4's tightened chain timing).
861	
862	Native GitHub issue dependencies (blocked-by/blocking — GA since Aug 2025,
863	API- and webhook-supported) and sub-issues *mirror* these fields: the tick
864	writes the native edge alongside the body field, buying the dependency UI for
865	free ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2). The body fields remain the truth the tick
866	parses — they are portable to any tracker with issues, labels, and comments,
867	which is the platform-agnosticism the sketch asks for. One vendored module owns
868	parse/serialize of the two fields; nothing else touches them.
869	
870	Cycles: the tick readies nothing in a `Blocked-by` cycle, forever, and the
871	stale escalation (§11) surfaces it as `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-action` after ~2 periods — the
872	same convergence-not-prevention posture as the rest of the system. The tick
873	does not attempt cycle detection; the janitor's health review may.
874	
875	## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism
876	
877	The default deployment stays one vendored cron workflow — the repo's only
878	cron, rule unchanged — containing the tick job and a drain (the tick runs
879	first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's
880	latency at zero even without events). Event triggers (`task:ready` labeled)
881	give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup — with one platform fact
882	worth knowing: a label written by a workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` emits no
883	triggering event (GitHub's recursion guard), so events only ever come from
884	*foreign* tokens — a human, a CLI on a PAT, an agent session. The drain being
885	in-run is what makes that harmless; it is the structural delivery, events the
886	sugar.
887	
888	**The capacity model, honestly** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the work
889	step is the work, so throughput is run *occupancy* — one run, one item, and
890	the queue drains as a chain of runs. The CCR sessions runs hand off
891	parallelize for free; the executor-side work does not. So executor width is
892	the primary capacity parameter, not a garnish: scale with a matrix width for
893	parallel executor jobs, or with executors outside Actions entirely — the
894	contract is "issue read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner
895	anywhere with a token qualifies. The chain itself is **self-re-dispatch**:
896	`workflow_dispatch` is one of the two event types a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can*
897	fire, so a run that ends with ready items left re-dispatches the executor
898	workflow and a fresh run continues.
899	One fairness note, accepted at today's scale: the randomized pick (§6.1)
900	removes any *systematic* head domination, but a heavy item still occupies its
901	run for the full work bound while light tasks wait out the chain — a sentence
902	here rather than machinery, until it is measured.
903	
904	**What starts an executor run is an enumerable list, and each cause is on the
905	record** (2026-08-15, and the sim asserts it — S34): (1) **the tick's own
906	drain job** — the guaranteed delivery, started by the cron workflow's job
907	graph (`needs: tick`), no event involved; (2) **a `task:ready`/`task:urgent`
908	label event** — foreign tokens only, the latency sugar; (3) **the close-time
909	drain** — whoever converges an item triggers a drain when anything is
910	pickable after its readiness re-check (§9); (4) **self-re-dispatch** — a run
911	that ends its one item with others still pickable dispatches a fresh run;
912	(5) **the failure continuation** — a run that dies (crash, timeout,
913	cancellation, runner loss) never reaches its re-dispatch, so the executor
914	workflow carries a second job, `needs: execute` with `if: failure() ||
915	cancelled()`, which the platform runs on a fresh runner and whose one step
916	re-dispatches — a dead run stalls the train by ~a minute, not until the next
917	cron fire (S36). Causes 3–5 ride `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
918	`GITHUB_TOKEN` *is* permitted to fire — the explicit exemption in the same
919	recursion guard that suppresses its label events — so no wider credential is
920	involved.
921	
922	**The tick must never wait on a drain** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15).
923	The heartbeat retires the sub-hour cap on executor runs (§6), and a long
924	drain sharing the tick's serializing `concurrency` group would then hold the
925	next cron fire — instantiation, readiness and the leash reclaim all stalling
926	behind the very work they schedule. So the serialization the double-tick
927	guard needs (S6) scopes to the **tick alone**, and executor work runs outside
928	it: the drain leaves the cron workflow's concurrency group (its own group, or
929	the separate executor workflow via dispatch). A deployment where the drain
930	can still block the tick is mis-wired even while nothing visibly fails.
931	
932	Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system never
933	enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.
934	
935	## 11. Recovery — what the janitor keeps, what dies
936	
937	| failure | today | proposed |
938	|---|---|---|
939	| scheduler/tick miss or late fire | run-ledger catch-up math | same property from the occurrence guard (§5) — the next tick instantiates the most recent occurrence only |
940	| double tick | concurrency group + slot-title search | concurrency group + occurrence-guard search (same window, same answer) |
941	| lost label event | janitor re-arm (remove/re-add), 20-min grace, bounded by stale escalation | **retired** — executors poll on the tick's cron; events are latency sugar, never the only delivery |
942	| duplicate events / racing executors | claim lease on one implicit executor | same lease, N executors — the loser picks a different item |
943	| executor died mid-claim | — (executor was a session; janitor reclaimed via `agent-running`) | **the tick** (owner, 2026-08-13): `task:executing` with no activity past ~1h → strip to `task:ready` with a comment, so a dead executor's item is back in the queue within ~2h rather than ~25h. An executor iteration is minutes, not hours, and a lease checked once a day is not a short lease |
944	| executor run died with items still queued | n/a (one implicit executor; the next slot was a day away) | **the failure-continuation job** (owner, 2026-08-15): `needs: execute`, `if: failure() \|\| cancelled()` re-dispatches on a fresh runner, so the *queue* resumes in ~a minute while the dead run's own item waits for the leash; the tick drain is the backstop when the whole workflow run is lost (§10, S36) |
945	| agent session died mid-run | janitor: stale `agent-running` → `needs-human` after ~3h | same, on `task:agent` (a hand-off comment names the session, so the janitor can say *which* session died) |
946	| CCR invocation lost | undetectable (label event fired into the void); surfaced only by re-arm/stale | **synchronous**: a refused call converges `needs-human` with the error at once; an unanswered call leaves the item with the agent and the agent leash settles it — one call per item, never retried (§6.6) |
947	| item never picked up | stale dispatch escalation, period parsed from the slot id's leading char | same escalation, period read from the task's declared `frequency` at HEAD (or a default for ad-hoc items) — no title parsing; the stale item converges `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-action` — the lane is not being drained and the fix is outside the item — and leaves the queue |
948	| dependency never resolves | n/a | **the stale-ready rule cannot see it** — a blocked item is never ready (F14, caught by the simulator against S18's claim). The janitor gains a third rule: a blocked item whose blockers have not resolved for ~2 days gets an escalation *comment* — labels untouched, so the item still proceeds by itself the moment its blockers resolve; a human who decides it is dead closes it by hand |
