Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the basics pack's RULES.md](../../RULES.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work.
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. (A hostname-apex helper passed its tests but mis-stripped `tel-aviv.gov.il` → `gov.il`; the gap only surfaced when the function was run over the actual list of existing URLs.) Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never pin a declaration to itself.** Asserting that a config/manifest field equals the literal it is declared with (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'open-pr')`, `assert.equal(pack.id, 'thing')`) restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and, worse, teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. Assert what can actually come apart — a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set. If a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. content.text: Now §16.4 — the permission check replaces the bare association test, and the read-failure split:

input.old_string:
The verdict happens where every verdict happens: **once, at pickup, on the
executor** (§6.4). The built-in task's precondition refuses three ways, each a plain
no-go that converges the item `outcome:obsolete` (an ad-hoc item has no anchor to
roll to, and a refusal is nobody's inbox — it closes rather than joining a triage
lane):

- the issue is closed, or no longer carries `claude-queued` — the request was
  withdrawn between adoption and pickup;
- the issue's `author_association` is not `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR`,
  **and** no comment from such an association matches the approval phrase
  `/claude go`;
- the issue cannot be read at all.

`author_association` is computed by GitHub from the asker's permission on the
repository and rides every issue and comment payload, so it is not forgeable by
anyone who can type — which is what lets "minimal security" be genuinely minimal.
The approval-comment path exists for the issue somebody else opened: a collaborator
blesses it without having to re-file it.
input.new_string:
The verdict happens where every verdict happens: **once, at pickup, on the
executor** (§6.4). The built-in task's precondition refuses three ways, each a plain
no-go that converges the item `outcome:obsolete` (an ad-hoc item has no anchor to
roll to, and a refusal is nobody's inbox — it closes rather than joining a triage
lane):

- the issue is closed, or no longer carries `claude-queued` — the request was
  withdrawn between adoption and pickup;
- neither the issue's author nor any commenter of the approval phrase
  `/claude go` **has push permission on the repository**;
- the issue is definitively **gone** — the API answers that it does not exist.

**Push permission is read from the permission API**
(`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{username}/permission`, requiring
`admin`, `maintain` or `write`), with the payload's `author_association` usable
only as a prefilter that saves the call. The association alone is deliberately
not the check: `MEMBER` is any org member whatever their repo permission, and
`COLLABORATOR` includes read-only collaborators — broader than the push access
the ask demands. Both facts are server-computed and unforgeable by anyone who
can type, which is what lets "minimal security" be genuinely minimal; the
permission read just makes the gate mean what it says. The approval-comment
path exists for the issue somebody else opened: someone with push blesses it
without having to re-file it — and the blessing is the *comment*, not the mark:
applying `claude-task` to another person's issue authorizes nothing by itself.

**A read failure is not a verdict.** A refusal's write-back (§16.5) cannot
reach an issue it cannot read, so declining on a transient API failure (a rate
limit, a 500) would strand `claude-queued` on the issue forever over nothing —
the request silently eaten. Only a definitive *gone* declines; any other read
failure **fails the run**: the item parks `needs-human` +

The verdict happens where every verdict happens: **once, at pickup, on the
executor** (§6.4). The built-in task's precondition refuses three ways, each a plain
no-go that converges the item `outcome:obsolete` (an ad-hoc item has no anchor to
roll to, and a refusal is nobody's inbox — it closes rather than joining a triage
lane):

- the issue is closed, or no longer carries `claude-queued` — the request was
  withdrawn between adoption and pickup;
- neither the issue's author nor any commenter of the approval phrase
  `/claude go` **has push permission on the repository**;
- the issue is definitively **gone** — the API answers that it does not exist.

**Push permission is read from the permission API**
(`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{username}/permission`, requiring
`admin`, `maintain` or `write`), with the payload's `author_association` usable
only as a prefilter that saves the call. The association alone is deliberately
not the check: `MEMBER` is any org member whatever their repo permission, and
`COLLABORATOR` includes read-only collaborators — broader than the push access
the ask demands. Both facts are server-computed and unforgeable by anyone who
can type, which is what lets "minimal security" be genuinely minimal; the
permission read just makes the gate mean what it says. The approval-comment
path exists for the issue somebody else opened: someone with push blesses it
without having to re-file it — and the blessing is the *comment*, not the mark:
applying `claude-task` to another person's issue authorizes nothing by itself.

**A read failure is not a verdict.** A refusal's write-back (§16.5) cannot
reach an issue it cannot read, so declining on a transient API failure (a rate
limit, a 500) would strand `claude-queued` on the issue forever over nothing —
the request silently eaten. Only a definitive *gone* declines; any other read
failure **fails the run**: the item parks `needs-human` +
`task:needs-human-failure`, open and visible, and the ordinary re-queue lever
(§4) retries it once the API recovers.

### S45 — an unauthorized mark is refused once, and disarmed

The same play with an issue opened by `NONE` and blessed by nobody. The tick
adopts it (adoption forms no judgment), the precondition declines, the item
**closes** `outcome:obsolete` — a refusal is nobody's inbox, so it joins no
triage lane — and the executor comments on #500 and removes `claude-queued`.
The disarm is the point: without it every tick for the rest of time re-adopts
and re-refuses the same issue.

### S46 — the approval path

An outsider's issue with `/claude go` from an `OWNER` runs and parks for
review. The same issue with `/claude go` from a `NONE` does not — the phrase
decides nothing on its own; the association behind it does.
input.new_string:
### S45 — an unauthorized mark is refused once, and disarmed

The same play with an issue opened by someone with no permission on the repo
and blessed by nobody. The tick adopts it (adoption forms no judgment), the
precondition declines, the item **closes** `outcome:obsolete` — a refusal is
nobody's inbox, so it joins no triage lane — and the executor comments on #500
and removes `claude-queued`. The disarm is the point: without it every tick
for the rest of time re-adopts and re-refuses the same issue.

### S46 — the approval path, judged by permission

An outsider's issue with `/claude go` from someone with push runs and parks
for review. The same issue with `/claude go` from someone without does not —
the phrase decides nothing on its own; the permission behind it does. And the
permission is the *API-read* permission, not the payload association (F30): a
read-only collaborator — who rides every payload as `COLLABORATOR` — is
refused on their own issue exactly like a stranger.

input.new_string:
### S49 — a broken request stays put; re-marking supersedes it

The session fails. The item parks at `task:needs-human-failure` — someone reads
the trace — and #500 keeps `claude-queued`: nothing mechanical re-arms work that
writes code, and that standing label is what stops the next tick adopting a
second run. The person fixes the cause and re-marks the issue: exactly one
further adoption, at whatever model the new label asks for — and that adoption
**supersedes the parked item** (F28), closing it `outcome:obsolete` with a
comment naming the re-ask, so the retry never leaves its predecessor parked
forever beside the run that replaced it.

### S50 — gone declines; unreadable fails the run

Two requests meet a broken read at pickup. One's issue is **gone** — the API
answers it does not exist: a plain decline, `outcome:obsolete`, no session, and
nothing to write back to. The other's issue exists but **cannot be read** — a
rate limit, a 500. Declining there would eat the request permanently (F27): the
decline's own write-back cannot reach the issue, so `claude-queued` would stand
forever over nothing. Instead the run **fails**: the item parks at
`task:needs-human-failure`, open and visible, the issue untouched and still
armed. The API recovers, a human re-queues the item (§4's lever, no new
adoption), and the run completes to its approval park.

### S51 — an impatient re-ask waits out the live run

`claude-task` is re-applied while the first run is still with its agent. The
mark **waits on the issue, unconsumed** — the ticks that fire mid-run adopt
nothing, because one issue gets one live item (F28) — and the tick that finds
the run settled (parked for review) supersedes that park and adopts the
waiting mark. Two runs, strictly in sequence, never two sessions on one issue.

1	# Task dispatch — scenario play-through
2	
3	Twenty scenarios played, minute by minute, against the mechanism exactly as
4	[DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) specifies it (owner request on #784: *"play them out
5	using this mechanism, and see if there are conceptual issues we missed"*).
6	Each scenario ends in a verdict: **holds** (the design handles it as written),
7	or a numbered **finding**. The findings ledger at the end classifies every
8	finding and says what was done about it — some amended DESIGN.md in this same
9	change, some are owner calls added to its §15.
10	
11	> **Read §H, then §I, for the current mechanism.** Sections A–G record rounds
12	> one and two (the tick-evaluates models); the owner's **standing-item model**
13	> (2026-08-13) replaced generation, and §H replays everything it touches. §I
14	> records the **work-as-work review** (2026-08-15) — the correction that the
15	> work step IS the work — and the invocation reversal (at-most-once, the
16	> agent lease deleted) decided the same day: where earlier sections conflict
17	> with §I, §I is the design as it stands. The superseded sections are kept
18	> because their reasoning is the record.
19	>
20	> **The scenarios are executable.** [`sim/`](sim/) holds a discrete-event
21	> simulator of the mechanism (virtual clock, no threads, no waits) and
22	> [`sim/scenarios.test.mjs`](sim/scenarios.test.mjs) plays the §H scenarios
23	> against it as `at time X, Y happens` tests, run by CI. A future design
24	> change should change the simulator first and let the red tests name the
25	> scenarios it breaks. Its first run caught F13 — a double-execution bug
26	> every prose replay had missed.
27	
28	## Cast and constants
29	
30	A fictional but realistic repo, tasks drawn from the real fleet:
31	
32	| task | frequency (anchor) | model | ceiling | notes |

36	| `grow/growth-promote` | daily (04:00Z) | opus | open-pr | canon repo; `after: ['grow/growth-extract']` |
37	| `tidy/tidy-issues` | daily (04:00Z) | sonnet | none | precondition: issue touched in window |
38	| `gcec/create-extractor` | hourly | sonnet | open-pr | code-work-heavy, conditional hand-off |
39	| `chrome/store-release` | daily (04:00Z) | none | none | agentless: code-work only |
40	| `sheepdog/fleet-baseline` | manual | sonnet | merged-pr | fan-out target |

# Writing migration and implementation plans

A plan's phases are not a narrative of the work; they are a **schedule of who has to be present
when**. Ordering them by topic — "phase 1: the store, phase 2: the workers, phase 3: cutover" —
scatters the moments that need a human across the whole run, and every one of them stops it. Order
them by *what blocks*, and the run ends with a stretch nobody has to attend.

Everything below assumes the change is already agreed: the problem, and that this migration is the
right way to solve it (basics' *Starting any requested change*). The end-state's **shape** —
converging in one forced pass, accepting legacy input at the door, a standing mechanism for
stragglers — is [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Planning a migration*; this skill is the ordering.

## The three blocks, and where each belongs

Sort every step of the plan into one of three kinds, and let that sort — not the subject matter —
decide the phase it lands in.

**1. Out-of-band setup — before any code changes.** Anything performed outside the repo that a
later step will need: provisioning an environment, creating a session or runner, setting a secret
or variable, granting a permission, flipping a platform setting, registering a webhook. Nearly all
of it is **non-destructive** — it adds a capability that nothing yet consumes, so doing it early
costs nothing and changes no behaviour. Doing it *late* costs the whole run: the plan reaches the
step that reads the secret and stops until someone is available.

Front-load all of it into phase zero, before the first line of code. Write it as its own issue
with a checkbox per step (basics' *Handing over a human-only step*), stating for each what stays
broken while it is off. And before writing it down, confirm you genuinely cannot do it yourself —
a step handed to a human that you could have taken is the most expensive kind of block there is.

The exception is the genuinely destructive step — deleting the old store, revoking the old
credential, removing the compatibility shim. Those are not setup; they are the migration's tail,
and they belong after the cutover has been observed working.

**2. Review and authorization gates — collapsed into one pass.** Every phase that ships code is a
gate: the owner must read it and approve it before the next phase can start. A plan with four
coding phases has four such waits, and each one is dead time whose length nobody controls.

Write **all** the code first, as a stack of PRs each based on the previous, and put the whole
stack in front of the owner together. The stack keeps the reviewable units small and independent —
one concern per PR, as ever — while costing one arrival of attention rather than four. Merge it
base-first once approved.

Approval of the stack is approval of the stack: it does not extend to a fix authored afterwards
(basics' *Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed*).

**3. Execution steps — whatever is left.** Once phase zero has landed the setup and the stack has
merged, the remaining steps run the migration: force the converge, backfill the members, watch the
cutover, retire the shim. If the first two sorts were done properly there is no gate among them —
they can be run at will, in one sitting, by whoever is at the keyboard.

That is the test of the plan. **Read the phases in order and mark every point where the run would
have to stop and wait for a person.** Each mark that falls after phase zero and the review pass is
a step that was sorted wrong. Move it, or say in the plan why it genuinely cannot move.

## Writing it down

- **The plan is a tracking issue**, and the phases are its checkboxes. Status and remaining work
  live there; a design document, where the project keeps one, carries the mechanism and not the
  progress.
- **Each phase names its exit condition**, observable and stated as a thing that reads back true —
  not "cutover done" but "every member's stamp shows the new ref". A phase whose end is a judgment
  call is a phase that stays open.
- **Nothing closes on a human's memory.** A step you cannot verify now gets a mechanism that comes
  to you — a scheduled task, a watched PR, an issue something converges (basics' *When verifying now
  is genuinely impossible*). A phase whose closing condition is "check next week" is not a phase.
- **Size each step to what it is**, and don't restate in the plan what the design document or the
  linked issue already carries.

## Working through the plan

Once the plan is agreed, the issue body's plan is **append-only**. While implementing, tick its
checkboxes and add below it — a comment, or a new section for what the work turned up — and never
edit, reword, condense or re-order what was already there.

The body is the record of what was agreed, and it is the only copy: an edit overwrites it in place
with nothing left to diff against, so a plan silently rewritten to match what was built reads
afterwards as a plan that was followed. Keeping it fixed is what makes the divergence visible —
and a divergence is the interesting part, not an embarrassment to tidy away.

So when the work shows a phase was wrong, say so **underneath**: what the plan assumed, what turned
out to be true, and what you did instead. If that changes the plan going forward, the new steps are
an addition, appended and dated; the superseded ones stay where they are, marked superseded rather
than deleted.

The exception is a **correction to the plan itself before implementation of it starts** — the owner
saying the plan misreads what they asked for. That is a correction (basics' *Acting on a
correction*): repair the body, since there is no work yet for it to have diverged from.

## Reviewing someone else's plan

Run the same sort over it. The findings worth raising, in order of what they cost:

1. A secret, permission, environment or account created **after** code that depends on it.
2. More than one review gate — two or more phases that each end in "open a PR and wait".
3. A destructive step scheduled before the replacement has been observed working.
4. A phase with no stated exit condition, or one only a person can judge.
5. A step handed to a human that the agent could have performed itself.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

1	// The work item — the queue's one durable object (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §3, §4).
2	// An issue titled `[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task> [qualifier]`, whose labels are
3	// its state, whose body's first line is the task path, and whose two optional body
4	// fields (`Not-before`, `Blocked-by`) are the only scheduling facts it carries.
5	//
6	// PURE, and deliberately the whole schema: everything else — anchors, guards,
7	// yields, leashes, verdicts — is computed fresh at every tick and pick from the
8	// engine and the declarations at HEAD (DESIGN §14). The label-and-field vocabulary
9	// here is therefore the compatibility surface across engine versions, which is why
10	// additive change is the strongly preferred shape and a rename needs a migration.
11	//
12	// Parse/serialize of the two fields lives here and nowhere else (DESIGN §9).
13	//
14	// The one import, and a frozen constant at that: the pack-rename map, which this
15	// module needs to keep reading titles written before a rename (see parseWorkItemTitle).
16	import { canonicalPackId } from '../../pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs';
17	
18	// The title prefix. Disjoint from the slot mechanism's `[claudinite-task]` on
19	// purpose: the two mechanisms coexist per-repo behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`,
20	// and neither may read the other's issues (DESIGN §14, S29).
21	export const WORK_PREFIX = '[claudinite-work]';
22	
23	export const BLOCKED = 'task:blocked';
24	export const READY = 'task:ready';
25	export const URGENT = 'task:urgent';
26	export const EXECUTING = 'task:executing';
27	export const AGENT = 'task:agent';
28	export const ORIGIN_SCHEDULE = 'origin:schedule';
29	export const NEEDS_HUMAN = 'needs-human';
30	
31	// The TRIAGE SUB-LABELS. `needs-human` says an item is parked; these say what the
32	// human parked with it is expected to DO, which is the whole difference between a
33	// queue a person can skim and one they have to read. Every park wears BOTH:
34	// `needs-human` stays the single state the machine reads (every guard, sweep and
35	// dashboard already turns on it), and the sub-label is the human's routing.
36	//
37	// The four are disjoint by REMEDY, not by cause:
38	//   action   — something outside the code must change: a secret set, a scope
39	//              granted, a routine's prompt or endpoint fixed, an item re-created
40	//              with the parameter it was missing. Mechanical; no judgement.
41	//   decision — the run stopped mid-flight and what happens next is a choice:
42	//              re-queue or abandon, does the half-done work stand, was the
43	//              ceiling violation acceptable.
44	//   approval — the run SUCCEEDED and deliberately left an unmerged PR. The only
45	//              park that is not a fault; the human merges it or closes it.
46	//   failure  — the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or
47	//              forged item. Someone diagnoses and fixes code.
48	// `failure` is the default a park falls back to, so an unclassified park reads as
49	// "diagnose me" rather than quietly joining the mechanical lane.
50	const triage = (kind) => `task:needs-human-${kind}`;
51	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION = triage('action');
52	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION = triage('decision');
53	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL = triage('approval');
54	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE = triage('failure');
55	export const TRIAGE_LABELS = Object.freeze([
56	  NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION, NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION, NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL, NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE,
57	]);
58	// WHICH PARKS HOLD THE TASK'S LANE. An open `origin:schedule` item IS the task's
59	// standing item, so while one exists the generator files no further occurrence
60	// (`planTick` job 1) — which for a park means the task stops being scheduled at
61	// all until a human clears it. That is right for a `failure`: filing a queue of
62	// items that will break the same way helps nobody, and the silence is the signal.
63	// It is wrong for the other three, which are a person's inbox, not a fault in the
64	// task: a PR waiting to be approved, a choice waiting to be made and a secret
65	// waiting to be set must not also stop tomorrow's run.
66	//
67	// A park wearing NO sub-label blocks, which is what makes this safe on the way in:
68	// every item parked by an engine older than the sub-labels, and every kind word a
69	// future engine invents that this one does not know, holds the lane rather than
70	// silently letting a broken task keep filing work.
71	export const isBlockingPark = (item) =>
72	  hasLabel(item, NEEDS_HUMAN)
73	  && !hasLabel(item, NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION)
74	  && !hasLabel(item, NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION)
75	  && !hasLabel(item, NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL);
76	
77	// A kind word (from a worker's own triage marker, or a call site) to its label.
78	// Anything unrecognised is a `failure`: a worker that misspells its class has a
79	// bug, which is exactly what that lane means.
80	export const triageLabelFor = (kind) =>
81	  (TRIAGE_LABELS.includes(triage(kind)) ? triage(kind) : NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE);
82	
83	export const OUTCOME_DONE = 'outcome:done';
84	// @deprecated Nothing writes this since the approval park: a run that left an
85	// unmerged PR no longer CLOSES as delivered, it parks at
86	// `task:needs-human-approval` and waits to be merged. Kept exported, kept in
87	// `QUEUE_LABELS`, and still read everywhere it was read — closed issues carrying
88	// it are stored data, and a decoder that stopped recognising it would turn every
89	// historical delivered run into an un-outcomed one.
90	export const OUTCOME_DELIVERED = 'outcome:delivered';
91	export const OUTCOME_OBSOLETE = 'outcome:obsolete';
92	
93	// The four state labels an open item may wear. An open item wearing none of them
94	// and no `needs-human` is off the state machine entirely — a torn label swap's
95	// leavings, which the janitor repairs (DESIGN §6.2, §11).
96	export const STATE_LABELS = [BLOCKED, READY, EXECUTING, AGENT];
97	
98	// Every label this mechanism applies, with the colour and description a bootstrap
99	// one-off would have given it. Ensured create-if-missing before anything is
100	// applied: GitHub 422s when you apply an unknown label and never creates one on
101	// demand, so the thing that assigns a label guarantees it first.
102	export const QUEUE_LABELS = [
103	  { name: BLOCKED, color: 'c5def5', description: 'Claudinite queue: waiting on Blocked-by and/or Not-before' },
104	  { name: READY, color: '0e8a16', description: 'Claudinite queue: available for an executor to pick up' },
105	  { name: URGENT, color: 'd93f0b', description: 'Claudinite queue: pick this before any non-urgent item' },
106	  { name: EXECUTING, color: 'fbca04', description: 'Claudinite queue: an executor holds the claim' },
107	  { name: AGENT, color: '1d76db', description: 'Claudinite queue: an agent session owns this item' },
108	  { name: ORIGIN_SCHEDULE, color: 'ededed', description: 'Claudinite queue: created by the generator tick at a task anchor' },
109	  { name: NEEDS_HUMAN, color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite queue: parked for a human — the one triage state' },
110	  { name: NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION, color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite triage: a human must change something outside the code' },
111	  { name: NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION, color: 'd93f0b', description: 'Claudinite triage: a human must choose what happens next' },
112	  { name: NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL, color: '5319e7', description: 'Claudinite triage: succeeded and left an unmerged PR to approve' },
113	  { name: NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE, color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite triage: the run broke — diagnose and fix' },
114	  { name: OUTCOME_DONE, color: '0e8a16', description: 'Claudinite queue: succeeded, nothing pending' },
115	  { name: OUTCOME_DELIVERED, color: '5319e7', description: 'Claudinite queue: succeeded and left a live artifact the world still has to act on' },
116	  { name: OUTCOME_OBSOLETE, color: 'ededed', description: 'Claudinite queue: never ran — the precondition said no, or the task is gone' },
117	];
118	
119	// GitHub hands labels back as objects on the issues API and as bare strings in
120	// some fixtures; accept either.
121	export const labelNames = (issue) =>
122	  (issue?.labels ?? []).map((l) => (typeof l === 'string' ? l : l?.name)).filter(Boolean);
123	
124	export const hasLabel = (issue, name) => labelNames(issue).includes(name);
125

content.text:
I have the full picture. Here's the overview.

## The label vocabulary, as the engine actually writes it

All of these are **live, fleet-wide stored data** — the queue is the only dispatch mechanism now (the slot scheduler is deleted), so every member carries these on open standing items and closed history. The single source is [`engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs) (`QUEUE_LABELS`, the ensured set).

**On work items (`[claudinite-work]` issues), machine-written — three namespaces:**

| label | namespace answers | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `task:blocked` / `task:ready` / `task:executing` / `task:agent` | *what state is it in* | the four states |
| `task:urgent` | | pick-order modifier |
| `task:needs-human-action` / `-decision` / `-approval` / `-failure` | | the four triage parks |
| `needs-human` | | **the one unprefixed state** — and it's already scheduled to die: [#1050](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1050) retires it as a written label by 2026-08-26, leaving the four `task:needs-human-*` as the park state |
| `outcome:done` / `outcome:obsolete` | *how did it end* (closed census) | queryable outcome mix |
| `outcome:delivered` | | retired 2026-08-19, read-only — closed issues carrying it are stored data |
| `origin:schedule` | *who created it* | the generator's dedup guards key on it |

**Designed but unbuilt (§16, [#1010](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1010)):** `origin:request` joins the work-item set; `claude-task`, `claude-model:{opus,sonnet,haiku}`, `claude-queued`, `claude-in-review` go on **ordinary issues**, person-applied from a phone.

**Old slot-mechanism leftovers** (`ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-agent-fleet`, `agent-running`, `workflow-failure`): historical data on old `[claudinite-task]` issues only; their constants linger in `dispatch.mjs` mainly because the janitor and the fleet-digest collector still import the shared `needs-human` from there.

## On prefixing everything with `task:`

Three things push back on the instinct:

1. **The prefix buys no query.** GitHub label filtering is exact-match only — there is no `label:task:*` wildcard in issue search — so a shared prefix is only an alphabetical grouping in the labels-management UI. The reliable "all queue issues" filter is the title prefix `[claudinite-work]`, and every label query stays exact whatever the spelling.
2. **After #1050 the inconsistency you're sensing is already gone.** `needs-human` is the only unprefixed work-item label, and #1050 retires it, leaving exactly three namespaces each answering a different question (state / ending / provenance). Folding `outcome:` and `origin:` under `task:` (`task:outcome:done`?) collapses that distinction for no query gain — and any rename is a fleet migration: a record relabeling open items on every member, decoders mapping every legacy spelling straight to today's (the #1013 lesson), a cross-repo reader sweep (fleet-digest reads `needs-human`), and `outcome:delivered` staying recognized under its old spelling forever regardless.
3. **The `claude-*` labels must stay out of `task:`.** §16.1 is explicit that a marked ordinary issue *never wears a `task:` label*, and that's load-bearing: the queue's guards and the janitor's stateless-item repair select on `task:*`, and keeping ordinary issues out of that vocabulary is what keeps them invisible to the queue's rules. They're also person-typed — short names are the feature.

questions.question: Why origin:schedule exists today: the guards must tell the task's STANDING item (consumes occurrences, rolls on no-go, holds the lane) from an AD-HOC item of the same task (invisible to occurrence accounting — #749's property). But that distinction is derivable from structure: an unqualified item of a task with a frequency IS the standing item; a qualified item, or an item of a manual task, is ad-hoc; a request item is known by its Request: field (so origin:request never gets built either). The roll-vs-close fork already derives from frequency at HEAD. The one semantic shift deletion forces: hand-creating an unqualified item of a scheduled task stops meaning "a parallel ad-hoc run" and becomes minting/waking the standing item — which §8 already made the sanctioned force lever; deliberate concurrency then requires a qualifier. Delete origin:schedule?

options.description: Matches the canon rule "prefer a structural classifier to a hand-set field". Guards key on the unqualified title + frequency at HEAD; #749's ad-hoc-parallel-run case is vestigial now that forcing is the wake lever. Costs a design/sim re-verification pass (S15/S17 replays) and, at implementation, a decoder that ignores the legacy label.

options.label: Keep it
options.description: Preserves the ability to run an unqualified ad-hoc item of a scheduled task beside its standing item without touching occurrence accounting. One hand-set classification, applied by the tick and the CLI, forever.

input.old_string:
**Origin marker.** Items the generator creates carry `origin:schedule`; items
created by hand, by a task, or by a fan-out do not, and an item adopted from a
marked issue carries `origin:request` (§16.3). The generator's dedup
guards (§5) count only `origin:schedule` items, so scheduled work and ad-hoc
work never suppress each other — a pending follow-up does not silence tomorrow's
occurrence, and an urgent hand-created item does not consume it either. A task
whose precondition should care about open follow-ups can see them through the
`issues` signal, as task-specific logic where it belongs.
input.new_string:
**Standing vs ad-hoc is structural — there is no origin marker** (owner,
2026-08-19; this deletes `origin:schedule`, and `origin:request` dies unbuilt).
An **unqualified** item of a task with a frequency *is* that task's standing
item: the guards (§5) key on the bare title and the frequency read at HEAD, so
nothing is hand-classified. Everything else is ad-hoc — an item of a `manual`
task, or any item carrying a qualifier — and sits outside the family by its
very title, so scheduled work and ad-hoc work never suppress each other: a
pending follow-up (its own task) does not silence tomorrow's occurrence, and a
fan-out target (qualified) does not consume it. Two consequences, both
deliberate: creating an unqualified item of a scheduled task where none is
open **is** minting its standing item — the same act as §8's force lever, not
a lookalike — so deliberate concurrency for one task always names a qualifier;
and a request item needs no marker either, being known by its `Request:` field
(§16.3). The fielded engine still applies `origin:schedule` until the
vocabulary migration; the label becomes inert stored data the decoders ignore.
A task whose precondition should care about open follow-ups can see them
through the `issues` signal, as task-specific logic where it belongs.

**Verdict: holds — today's parity, by ruling.**

### S13′ — "obsolete at pickup" becomes the roll

- Old S13: precondition true at creation, false at pickup → close
  `outcome:obsolete`. Under the standing-item model there *is* no creation
  verdict; the pick verdict is the only one, and a scheduled no-go rolls
  instead of closing. `outcome:obsolete` narrows to: task gone from the repo
  (S20), and ad-hoc items whose reason to exist lapsed (S17's follow-up
  finding the store already live). F2 ("an occurrence that fires-and-obsoletes
  is spent") dissolves — there is no fire-then-obsolete path left for
===
(S9a/S9b), the duplicate-session agent lease (S10), agent death and the
janitor's leash (S11), the force-while-executing mutex (S15), the lost label
event (S16), the follow-up (S17/S17b), the fan-out with a stuck member
(S18), and the human re-queue (S19). Making them executable found two
deltas and one more spec bug:

- **S12′ (delta):** old S12 ends with the re-queued item closing
  `outcome:obsolete`; under the standing-item model the re-ask's no-go
  **rolls** the scheduled item instead — same safety (the precondition
  re-run is still what makes crash-retry safe), better record (the reason
  and the next wake live on the item).
- **S24 (delta):** with F14's sweep in place, the blocked-by starvation is
  no longer *silent* — it surfaces as a stuck-dependency comment, days
  late. Still the wrong wiring; the yield stands.
===

- **S30 / F16 — a stale issue list duplicates the standing item.** The
  occurrence guards assume the tick's REST list sees an item created by a
  prior run. GitHub documents no such cross-node freshness bound. Rather
  than assume, the tick self-heals: more than one open family item → close
  all but the oldest, `outcome:obsolete`, dedupe comment.
- **S31 / F17 — the leash arithmetic.** A code-work bound that reaches the
  executing leash is reclaimed *alive*, and the failure mode is a
  **livelock**, not one duplicate: every tenure is reclaimed before it can
===
consequences of there being one word.

### S40 — the lane rule, from both sides (replaces an assertion, not a scenario)

The finding that started it (**F25**) was not simulated at all: it was
measured in production. An open `origin:schedule` item *is* its task's standing
item, so any park stopped the task being scheduled — `missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
`fleet-digest` failed once on a permission gap, its item sat parked, and **no
item was ever filed behind it for two days** while the four sweeps whose items
had closed kept running normally. The dashboard read healthy and the series
simply stopped.

than closing, and #500 moves to `claude-in-review`. A further day of ticks

1	# Task dispatch — scenario play-through
2	
3	Twenty scenarios played, minute by minute, against the mechanism exactly as
4	[DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) specifies it (owner request on #784: *"play them out
5	using this mechanism, and see if there are conceptual issues we missed"*).
6	Each scenario ends in a verdict: **holds** (the design handles it as written),
7	or a numbered **finding**. The findings ledger at the end classifies every
8	finding and says what was done about it — some amended DESIGN.md in this same
9	change, some are owner calls added to its §15.
10	
11	> **Read §H, then §I, for the current mechanism.** Sections A–G record rounds
12	> one and two (the tick-evaluates models); the owner's **standing-item model**
13	> (2026-08-13) replaced generation, and §H replays everything it touches. §I
14	> records the **work-as-work review** (2026-08-15) — the correction that the
15	> work step IS the work — and the invocation reversal (at-most-once, the
16	> agent lease deleted) decided the same day: where earlier sections conflict
17	> with §I, §I is the design as it stands. The superseded sections are kept
18	> because their reasoning is the record.
19	>
20	> **The scenarios are executable.** [`sim/`](sim/) holds a discrete-event
21	> simulator of the mechanism (virtual clock, no threads, no waits) and
22	> [`sim/scenarios.test.mjs`](sim/scenarios.test.mjs) plays the §H scenarios
23	> against it as `at time X, Y happens` tests, run by CI. A future design
24	> change should change the simulator first and let the red tests name the
25	> scenarios it breaks. Its first run caught F13 — a double-execution bug
26	> every prose replay had missed.
27	
28	## Cast and constants
29	
30	A fictional but realistic repo, tasks drawn from the real fleet:
31	
32	| task | frequency (anchor) | model | ceiling | notes |
33	|---|---|---|---|---|
34	| `basics/baselining` | daily-2h (02:00Z) | sonnet | merged-pr | code-work converges the mount; conditional hand-off |
35	| `grow/growth-extract` | daily-1h (03:00Z) | opus | merged-pr | `after: ['basics/baselining']` |
36	| `grow/growth-promote` | daily (04:00Z) | opus | open-pr | canon repo; `after: ['grow/growth-extract']` |
37	| `tidy/tidy-issues` | daily (04:00Z) | sonnet | none | precondition: issue touched in window |
38	| `gcec/create-extractor` | hourly | sonnet | open-pr | code-work-heavy, conditional hand-off |
39	| `chrome/store-release` | daily (04:00Z) | none | none | agentless: code-work only |
40	| `sheepdog/fleet-baseline` | manual | sonnet | merged-pr | fan-out target |
41	
42	Constants: tick cron minute **:17** (hourly); executor = post-tick drain job +
43	`task:ready`-labeled event runs; janitor = a daily item around 04:00; leashes —
44	`task:executing` 1h, `task:agent` 3h, unpicked-`task:ready` ~2 periods; work-step
45	heartbeat every **15m** (§I). "E1/E2" are executor iterations (workflow runs);
46	"the API" is the CCR routine-fire call, made **once per item, never retried** (§I).
47	
48	---
49	
50	## A. Routine nights
51	
52	### S1 — quiet night, nothing to do
53	
54	- **02:17** tick: baselining — occurrence guard passes (no item ≥ 02:00),
55	  backlog guard passes, precondition: mount converged yesterday, stamp fresh →
56	  `run: false`. No item. Same for every other task at its hour.
57	- **03:17–23:17** nothing re-evaluates: each occurrence had its one verdict at
58	  the first tick at-or-after its anchor, and a no-go spends it. Zero items
59	  created, zero further preconditions run, all day.
60	
61	**Verdict: holds.** *(Replayed after the 2026-08-13 go/no-go ruling. As first
62	drafted, the design re-evaluated every unfired occurrence each tick — 24
63	precondition runs and signal collections per quiet daily task, a ~×20 read
64	amplification, which is what F10 asked about. The ruling removed both the cost
65	and the question: one occurrence, one verdict.)*
66	
67	### S2 — happy path, one agentic task
68	
69	- **04:02** a contributor closes two issues; **04:17** tick: tidy-issues
70	  precondition sees issues touched in window → item #900 created,
71	  `task:ready`, Context naming the two issues.
72	- **04:17:40** the tick's own executor job drains: picks #900, lease
73	  (read/swap/comment/re-read) — clean claim, `task:executing`.
74	- **04:18** precondition re-run: still true; Context refreshed (same two
75	  issues). No code-work declared. Hand-off: body gets its sections, swap to
76	  `task:agent`, hand-off comment, API call → session `s-123`.
77	- **04:34** agent validates the item in code, triages the two issues within
78	  Context, verifies ceiling (`none`: no PR opened — ok), comments the result,
79	  closes #900 `outcome:done`, prints the exec record, captures.
80	
81	**Verdict: holds.** One item, one claim, one session, one terminal state, all
82	of it readable on #900.
83	
84	### S3 — work appears mid-window
85	
86	- **04:17** tidy-issues precondition: nothing touched → no-go. The occurrence
87	  is spent.
88	- **09:03** someone updates an old issue. **09:17** tick: the evaluate-once
89	  gate holds (this occurrence already had its verdict) → nothing happens.
90	- **Tomorrow 04:17** the next occurrence evaluates, sees the issue touched
91	  inside its window, and runs.
92	
93	**Verdict: holds, with the accepted latency.** *(Replayed after the go/no-go
94	ruling, which reversed this scenario's original outcome — it used to fire at
95	09:20.)* The work waits up to a day; the window-scoped signals mean it is
96	found, not lost. A task for which that latency is wrong declares a finer
97	`frequency` — which is what create-extractor's `hourly` already does, and is
98	the mechanism's own answer rather than a special case. Note this is exactly
99	today's behaviour, so it is parity, not a regression.
100	
101	## B. Scheduler unreliability
102	
103	### S4 — the late-fire night (the exclusive-claim replacement, end to end)
104	
105	GitHub drops the 02:17, 03:17 and 04:17 fires; the first tick lands **05:41**.
106	
107	- **05:41** tick job 1, iterating in dependency order (**F9** — see below):
108	  - baselining: A = 02:00, no item since → precondition true (stamp stale) →
109	    item #910, `task:ready`.
110	  - growth-extract: A = 03:00 → true; `after: [basics/baselining]` and #910 is
111	    open → item #911, `task:blocked`, `Blocked-by: #910`.
112	  - growth-promote: A = 04:00 → true; `after` extract, #911 open → #912
113	    blocked by #911.
114	  - tidy-issues, store-release: independent → #913, #914 `task:ready`.
115	- **05:42** executors drain: #910 claimed (baselining), #913, #914 run in
116	  parallel — they never depended on the mount ordering. Baselining's code-work
117	  converges the mount **06:02**; no judgment needed → no hand-off; closes
118	  #910 `outcome:done` **06:03**.
119	- **06:17** tick job 2: #911's blocker closed → `task:ready`; picked 06:18;
120	  extract's agent lands its PR **06:55**, closes #911 `outcome:done`.
121	- **07:17** tick readies #912; promote runs **07:20**.
122	
123	**Verdict: holds, and strictly better than today.** Today this night either
124	runs the chain *beside* baselining (pre-exclusive) or baselining claims the
125	run and extract/promote **lose the whole day** (deferred slots are spent).
126	Here the chain completes the same morning, ordered, ~1h of tick-quantized
127	latency per link. Two findings anyway:
128	
129	- **F9 (bug in the design as written):** §5's pseudocode iterates
130	  `discoverTasks()` in arbitrary order. If growth-extract is processed
131	  *before* baselining in the same tick, `openScheduledItemsOf(after)` finds
132	  nothing — baselining's item doesn't exist yet — and extract is created
133	  `task:ready`, running beside the mount converge. Job 1 must iterate in
134	  topological order of `after` edges (cycles: fall back to declaration order
135	  and warn). *Amended in DESIGN.md §5.*
136	- **F1 (optimization, not defect):** dependency readiness is quantized to the
137	  tick — each chain link waits for the next :17. Optional improvement, same
138	  event+poll shape as pickup: the converger, on closing an item, checks in
139	  code for open `task:blocked` items naming it and readies those whose

input.body:
DESIGN §15.25/§15.26 (owner, 2026-08-19; landed by #1063) renamed the terminal labels and deleted the origin marker. The fielded engine still writes the old vocabulary — this issue is the engine-side migration. Labels are stored data fleet-wide, so the rename follows the stored-data rule: decoders map every legacy spelling straight to today's, in one pass.

- [ ] `engine/scheduler/queue/work-item.mjs` — `OUTCOME_DONE` → `task:done`, `OUTCOME_OBSOLETE` → `task:obsolete`; drop `ORIGIN_SCHEDULE` from writes and from `QUEUE_LABELS`; keep reading every legacy spelling (`outcome:done`, `outcome:obsolete`, `outcome:delivered`, and `origin:schedule` as an inert no-op) — a decoder that stopped recognising them would turn historical runs into un-outcomed ones.
- [ ] Standing vs ad-hoc derives structurally everywhere the tick/executor branched on the marker: unqualified title + frequency at HEAD = the standing item; manual or qualified = ad-hoc; a request item by its `Request:` field (once #1010 lands it).

- [ ] A migration record: strip `origin:schedule` from open items and relabel open items' terminal expectations — closed history stays as-is (decode-side acceptance covers it).
- [ ] Ensure-set: `task:done`/`task:obsolete` created; `origin:schedule` no longer ensured.
- [ ] Timing: ride the same convergence window as #1050 (the `needs-human` pair collapse) so the fleet pays one relabel pass, not two.

Refs #1063, #1050, #1010.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.
